documents.title: Mohs micrographic surgery
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Mohs Surgery Report
Date: 01/11/2024
Diagnosis: invasive squamous cell carcinoma, well differentiated, right dorsal forearm (biopsy 12/04/2023).
Allergies: NKDA.

Pre-op lesion 2.0 cm. Local anesthesia.
Stage 1: tumor present at one deep edge. Stage 2: clear on all margins.
Final defect 3.1 x 2.6 cm, repaired with layered (intermediate) closure. Estimated blood loss minimal.
Wound care reviewed; sutures out in 14 days.

Plan: full skin checks every 6 months given his immunosuppression. Sun protection reviewed.
Mohs Surgery / Dermatology

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Mohs done in Jan, forearm healed with a neat scar. CT in Jan clear. Feeling well, training for a spring half.
He's been thinking about his heart since his dad's MI at 62 (he's 58) and wants a cardiology opinion. Also heard about another big trial of a new cholesterol medicine and wonders if he'd qualify.
Meds unchanged. NKDA.
O: BP and HR as charted. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Forearm scar well healed, no nodules. No edema.
A/P
- Lipids/CV risk: LDL has been ~120 on atorvastatin 40. Referral to cardiology for a risk review as he asked; lipids today for them.
- SCC R forearm s/p Mohs - moved to history. Derm checks q6 mo.
- Lung ca stage IA2 s/p lobectomy, NED.
- HTN controlled.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology Consultation
Date: 05/31/2024
Referred by primary care for cardiovascular risk review.

Mr. Moran is 58, a kidney transplant recipient (2018) with hypertension (transplant renal artery stent 2022), hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 40 mg, resected early-stage lung adenocarcinoma, cutaneous SCC treated with Mohs, and a former 25 pack-year smoker. Father had an MI at 62. He has no chest pain, exertional symptoms or palpitations and runs several days a week.

Medications: tacrolimus 5 mg BID, prednisone 5 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, naproxen sodium 220 mg BID as needed, albuterol as needed.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP and heart rate normal. Regular rhythm, no murmur. Carotids without bruit. Lungs clear. No edema.
Lipids (03/2024, primary care): LDL about 120.

He asked about enrolling in a large multicenter outcomes trial comparing a new lipid-lowering agent with statin therapy. We reviewed what participation would involve, including several years of visits, blinded assignment and frequent blood draws. Given the visit burden with his work and his transplant care, he decided not to enroll.

Impression: elevated cardiovascular risk, asymptomatic. Continue atorvastatin 40 mg daily and current blood pressure regimen. Follow up with us as needed.
Cardiology

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency Department Physician Record
Arrival: 11/28/2024 15:40

CC: vomiting blood, black stools.
HPI: 59-year-old man with a kidney transplant and a history of peptic ulcer disease vomited blood twice and passed black stool over the last two hours. A sharp, gnawing upper abdominal pain has been building over the past week. He has been taking over-the-counter naproxen frequently for knee pain while training. Also on daily prednisone.
Meds: tacrolimus, prednisone, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, naproxen OTC, albuterol prn.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 90/60, HR 120. Pale and diaphoretic. Abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness; no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly.
Labs: hemoglobin 9.4. INR normal.

ED course: two large-bore IVs, crystalloid bolus with improvement in pressure, IV pantoprazole bolus and infusion, type and cross. GI consulted for endoscopy. Admitted to medicine.
Impression: acute upper GI hemorrhage, likely peptic ulcer, NSAID-associated.

documents.title: Upper endoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy
Date: 11/29/2024
Indication: hematemesis and melena.
Allergies: NKDA. Moderate sedation.
Findings: Esophagus normal. Stomach with a small amount of old blood, mucosa otherwise normal; biopsies of antrum and body for H. pylori. Duodenal bulb: 1.5 cm ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel. Second portion normal.
Therapy: dilute epinephrine injection around the vessel, then two hemostatic clips. Good hemostasis.
Impression: duodenal bulb ulcer with non-bleeding visible vessel, treated endoscopically.
Recommendations: high-dose PPI, avoid all NSAIDs, follow biopsy results.
Addendum 12/02: gastric biopsies negative for Helicobacter pylori.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Discharge Summary
Admitted 11/28/2024, discharged 12/01/2024.
Diagnosis: acute upper GI hemorrhage from a duodenal bulb ulcer, NSAID-associated, H. pylori negative.

Course: Hemoglobin 9.4 on arrival, 8.3 the next morning; transfused 1 unit packed red cells. EGD 11/29 with epinephrine and clips to a visible vessel. No rebleeding. Diet advanced. Tacrolimus and prednisone continued; antihypertensives held on day 1 and resumed day 2 as pressures recovered. Creatinine at baseline.

Discharge medications:
NEW pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, then stop if off NSAIDs (review with PCP)
NEW ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for 3 months
STOP naproxen and all NSAIDs
CONTINUE tacrolimus 5 mg BID, prednisone 5 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, albuterol as needed
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with CBC.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: TCM call 2 days after discharge. No vomiting, stools turning brown. Some fatigue. Taking pantoprazole twice a day and iron. Knows to stop naproxen. Has not driven since. Appt 12/6 with PCP, CBC that day. Return precautions for black stool, vomiting blood, fainting.

medications.sig: Take 1 to 2 tablets by mouth every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, no more than 6 tablets a day

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 1 week after admission for a bleeding duodenal ulcer (11/28-12/1). Records reviewed: EGD with visible vessel, clipped; 1 unit PRBC; H. pylori neg.
Now: no further black stools since 11/30, no vomiting. Tired but improving. No lightheadedness. Taking pantoprazole BID and ferrous sulfate; mild constipation from iron.
He was taking a lot more naproxen than I realized during his training. We went over why it can't come back - ulcer history plus prednisone.
Meds: tacrolimus 5 BID, prednisone 5, amlodipine 10, HCTZ 25, atorvastatin 40, pantoprazole 40 BID, ferrous sulfate 325 daily, albuterol prn. NKDA.
Exam: BP/HR as charted, no orthostasis. Mild pallor. Abdomen soft, nontender. Heart regular.
Hgb today 11.4.
A/P
1. Duodenal ulcer bleed, NSAID-related: complete 8 wks pantoprazole BID. Naproxen removed from list - no NSAIDs at all, including OTC. Will reassess PPI at end of course.
2. Blood loss: Hgb recovering, iron x 3 months, CBC in ~2 months.
3. Knee pain: acetaminophen up to 3 g/day.
4. Off driving another week.
